extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students (those assessing or litigating patent damages)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and principles for proving and measuring damages for patent infringement, including when royalties, lost-profits/monopoly measures, or reasonable royalties apply, and related evidentiary rules and limits on recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary methods for assessing patent damages
rubrics_metrics.description: There are several methods of assessing damages for infringements of patents: (1) using the plaintiff's established royalty as the measure of those damages, (2) ascertaining what the defendant's interference with the plaintiff's close monopoly prevented the latter from deriving (lost profits/monopoly damages), and (3) proving what would have been a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these three criteria separately and in the stated order; each has distinct proof burdens and applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant's profits not direct measure of plaintiff's damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of the profits which the defendant derived from his infringement has no direct relevancy to the question of the plaintiff's damages in an action at law; defendant's profits as such are not recoverable in an action at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant's profits may be relevant in equity where the patentee elects to recover infringer's profits, but if the patentee elects that remedy he cannot also recover legal damages for same infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Established royalty must be uniform and pre-existing
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant may successfully object to a given royalty as a measure of the plaintiff's damages unless it was uniform, and was actually paid or secured before the defendant's infringement was committed by a sufficient number of persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniformity and prior payment/assurance by a sufficient number of licensees demonstrates that purchasers who need the license can afford to pay that royalty; absence permits defendant to object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single license insufficient to establish a royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale of a single license is not sufficient to establish a royalty because one purchaser may have paid more than others could afford.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple, consistent license transactions are required; courts look for substantial acquiescence by a number of licensees rather than an isolated contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath/testimony may prove an established royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: The oath and not the license being the best evidence of the royalty, the royalty may be proved by the oath without production of the license, even where the license is in writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavit or testimony attesting that the ostensible price was the true price can establish the royalty where licenses are unavailable or suspect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty must be uniform to bind third-party infringers; variation excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: A royalty, in order to be binding on a defendant who was a stranger to the licenses which established it, must be a uniform royalty. Variant rates (e.g., given for variant ability of licensees) are excluded from consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee may change the rate if enough licensees acquiesce to the new rate, but inconsistent rates across licensees undermine use of any particular rate against an unrelated infringer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty established after the infringement is inapplicable
rubrics_metrics.description: A particular royalty may be successfully objected to by a defendant if it was not established until after the infringement sued upon was committed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing matters — only royalties established prior to the infringing acts can serve as measures of damages for those acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial limits on established royalties
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff may successfully object where a royalty was established and intended to be established within a particular territory only; an Oregon royalty is not to be forced upon infringement committed in Minnesota, for example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Royalty rates tied to specific geographic markets cannot presumptively be applied to infringements occurring elsewhere without proof that the rate reflects the market for the infringement's location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changed or abandoned royalties before infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff may object to using a particular royalty where it was changed or abandoned before the infringement in suit was committed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical business reasons (poverty, misfortune) may justify later changes, but only contemporaneous established rates are generally applicable to prior infringements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compromise payments for past infringement do not establish royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Money paid for infringement already committed does not establish nor tend to establish a royalty; compromise payments may be larger or smaller than a proper royalty for various nonroyalty reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Settlement amounts reflect bargaining, fear of treble damages, insolvency, or litigation-avoidance and therefore are unreliable as measures of a true license royalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty reserved as part of patent purchase price is not proper measure
rubrics_metrics.description: A royalty which is reserved as the whole or a part of the purchase price of a patent is not a proper one to measure damages as against an infringer; it may be too large or too small for that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purchase-price-based royalties reflect transfer considerations (close monopoly, resale margins) and do not reliably indicate license value against third-party infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mismatch of license scope and infringement type invalidates using that royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: A royalty provided for in licenses to make and use is no measure of damages for an infringement which consisted of making and selling; similarly, licenses to make and sell specimens do not measure injury from making/using specimens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The nature of authorized acts in establishing licenses must correspond to the infringing acts whose damages are measured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality of damages to extent/duration of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an infringement was smaller in extent or shorter in duration than the corresponding doings authorized by the licenses which established the royalty, damages should be assessed at a correspondingly smaller sum (and vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust established royalties upward or downward to reflect relative scope/duration differences unless special facts render extent immaterial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial appropriation and apportionment among inventions/patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Where only part of the inventions covered by a particular patent are unlawfully appropriated, the infringer is liable for only an equitable proportion of the royalty established for all of those inventions jointly; when several patents' inventions were jointly licensed, divide the royalty into portions proportionate to the value of the several inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must furnish data/evidence to support any division or apportionment; absent data, courts will not make speculative allocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost-profits (monopoly) measure when no established royalty applies
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no established royalty is applicable, damages may be ascertained by finding what the plaintiff would have derived from his monopoly if the defendant had not interfered (lost sales and price reductions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the sum of profits the patentee would have made from sales the infringer prevented and the loss from any price reductions caused by the infringer; apportion total profits to the invention where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of proof for lost sales / lost-profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof of lost sales includes evidence showing (1) what profits the patentee would have derived from the sales the infringer prevented; (2) that the patentee could have supplied the articles; (3) that infringer's sales were to persons who would have bought from the patentee; and (4) that the infringer would have purchased from the patentee rather than gone without.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first three elements must be direct and strong; the last two need not be direct but must be legitimate circumstantial evidence. Where infringement was wanton, these evidentiary requirements may be relaxed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of reduced prices as an element of lost-profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of price reduction must show that the defendant's infringement caused or helped cause the reduction and must show the extent of the reduction so caused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include evidence merely that the patentee would have been asked to supply particular demand; must link price reduction causally to defendant's conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominal damages when conventional measures fail
rubrics_metrics.description: Where damages cannot be assessed on the basis of a royalty, nor on that of lost sales, nor on that of hurtful competition, only nominal damages can be recovered for the infringement of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff bears burden to fit the case into recognized measures; absent fit, recovery is limited to nominal compensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages for making specimens without sale are nominal absent proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages for infringement by making, without unlawfully selling or using, specimens of a patented thing will be nominal only unless there is an established royalty for such making, or a reasonable royalty can be shown, or some definite damage is proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making alone rarely yields substantial damages unless specific license practice or other proof supports valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages evidence must be reasonably definite (no conjecture)
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence of damages must be reasonably definite to justify a jury in finding a verdict for more than a nominal amount; conjecture is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If plaintiff shows damages were large and offers as accurate evidence as case permits, and defendant offers no counter-evidence (or withholds info), the jury should estimate damages on plaintiff's evidence and resolve uncertainties against the defendant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote consequential damages are not recoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: Remote consequential pecuniary injuries (e.g., business outside the patent injured, forced sale of unpatented property at less than value, borrowing at excessive rates, encouragement of other infringers from whom recovery cannot be obtained, loss from inability to attend other business) are too indirect to furnish a proper basis for recoverable damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus recovery on direct pecuniary injury caused by the infringement; consequential or speculative chain losses will likely be excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable royalty as alternative when no established royalty or lost sales
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff has not availed himself of patent rights by granting licenses (or license fees are not uniform) and there is no proof of lost sales or injury by competition, the plaintiff must prove what would have been a reasonable royalty for the defendant to pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining reasonable royalty is inherently an estimate; courts may look to prior established royalties, allow room for usual business profit and production cost, disentangle mixed 'rent and royalty' sums, and will not base reasonable royalty on defendants' profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant's profits not an element in reasonable royalty calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of the defendants' profits could not be taken as an element in determining a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasonable royalty focuses on license value, market bearing price, and established licensing practices rather than defendant profit figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemplary/punitive damages not for jury; judge may increase up to treble
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemplary damages cannot lawfully be given by a jury for any infringement of a patent; the power to inflict punitive damages is committed by statute to the judge, who may enter judgment for a sum above the verdict, not exceeding three times that amount, together with costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge may exercise this power where circumstances (deliberate/intentional infringement, bad faith, stubborn litigation, causing unnecessary trouble/expense) warrant; mere extensive defense requiring expense is not sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increased damages to prevent infringer profiting from wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: Increased damages may be awarded where necessary to prevent a defendant infringer from profiting from his own wrong, whether intentional or unwitting; the power is general and to be exercised according to circumstances of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts view this as equitable correction to avoid rewarding infringement; increased damages are not forfeitures and do not permit withholding testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravation by unfair competition may support additional recovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a defendant has infringed and also copied plaintiff's structure so closely as to be chargeable with unfair competition, damages for unfair competition may be recovered in the infringement suit as an aggravation of the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such recovery may be permitted irrespective of parties' citizenship (per cited circuit precedent) because unfair competition aggravates the infringement harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant's ignorance of the patent is not a defense; constructive notice
rubrics_metrics.description: A verdict for actual damages cannot be averted by evidence that the defendant was ignorant of the existence of the patent at the time he infringed; all infringers have constructive notice because patents are recorded in the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ignorance does not affect liability for actual damages, though deliberate continued infringement after validity is established will resolve factual doubts against the infringer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counsel fees and litigation expenses excluded from actual damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither counsel fees nor any other expenses incident to litigation can be included in a verdict for actual damages in a patent case; such fees may be recoverable only as costs per governing rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between damages (compensation for injury) and taxable costs/fee-shifting mechanisms; do not include litigation expenses in damage calculations.
